uae-japan-space-resources.story:
These are laws from the United Arab Emirates and Japan that allow companies to use materials mined in space, following the United States in 2015 and Luxembourg in 2017. The Emirates was also working with a private Japanese company on a Moon landing planned for 2022.

The Emirates' Federal Law No. 12 of 2019 is a general space law. It covers licensing, registering spacecraft, liability and insurance, along with rules on building facilities on other planets and on using space resources. It had come into force by early 2020. Japan's parliament, the Diet, then passed Act No. 83 of 23 June 2021, on business activities in exploring and developing space resources, which made Japan the fourth country to pass such a law. It took effect six months after it was published. Article 5 says that a licensed operator acquires ownership of resources it has mined under its approved business plan by possessing them with the intention to own them. Article 6 says that enforcing the Act must not hinder Japan's carrying out of its international agreements. The news site Atalayar describes the law as covering minerals from the surface and subsurface of the Moon, Mars or other bodies. Japan's Hayabusa 2 mission had returned a few grams of dust from the asteroid Ryugu in December 2020, which showed that extraction is possible on a small scale.

The legal idea is that national practice can gradually shape international law. Treaties are one source of international law, and another is custom, the consistent practice of states that they treat as lawful. When several countries pass similar laws and others do not object, this can start to count as custom. Together with the American and Luxembourg laws, these acts form a growing group of countries treating mining as a lawful use of space. The Emirates and Japan were also among the eight original signatories of the Artemis Accords on 13 October 2020, and 78 countries had signed by 28 October 2026. Signatories affirm that extracting and using space resources does not inherently constitute national appropriation. Critics argue that the Accords violate the Outer Space Treaty, and the legal status of space mining remains unclear, so a rule formed in this way has not yet been established.

No international treaty authorises this. Article II of the Outer Space Treaty still bars any country from claiming a body in space, and these laws give ownership of materials and not of ground. A person living at a mine on the Moon under these laws would remain under the licensing country's supervision. No court has tested the laws.
uae-japan-space-resources.why: Article 5 and Article 6 were paraphrased through a news site. Replaced with the text of the official translation, and added the Act's date and start.

ras-el-hekma.story:
Ras El-Hekma is a stretch of Egypt's Mediterranean coast about 350 kilometres north-west of Cairo. In February 2024 the governments of Egypt and the United Arab Emirates signed a $35 billion agreement over it, with the Emirates represented by a consortium led by ADQ, a state investment fund based in Abu Dhabi. It is on the map because of the size of the deal and the question of what such a payment actually buys.

The money came in two parts. ADQ was to pay $24 billion for the rights to develop the area, and to convert $11 billion of deposits it held into investments in projects elsewhere in Egypt. The plan covers more than 170 million square metres, or about 170 square kilometres, to be built up as a holiday destination, financial centre and free zone, an area with special business and tax rules. Egypt keeps a 35 per cent stake in the development. The UAE's investment minister described it as support for Egypt's economy.

In October 2024 ADQ appointed the Abu Dhabi developer Modon Holding as master developer for the whole area. Modon was to build a first phase of 50 million square metres, and private developers were to build the remaining 120 million under the supervision of Modon and an ADQ subsidiary. In May 2025 an Egyptian cabinet spokesman said Egypt had begun handing over plots and that Emirati developers had started initial work. In September 2025 the Egyptian outlet Al Manassa, citing an unnamed source, reported that building on the first phase had reached 5 per cent. In January 2026 Modon awarded Orascom a construction contract of E£15 billion, about $316 million, and it put out further tenders that month.

What passed here is development rights, the right to build on and profit from land, with Egypt as a partner. The announcement does not mention handing over the right to rule.
ras-el-hekma.why: The entry stopped at the February 2024 announcement. Added what has happened since.

add_sources.t: ADQ and Modon sign Ras El-Hekma development deals, MEED, 7 Oct 2024
Ras El-Hekma's $35B megaproject lags, Al Manassa, 2 Sep 2025
Modon tenders Ras El-Hekma construction contracts, MEED, 6 Feb 2026

isle-of-man-revestment.story:
The Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea, was for a long time ruled under the Crown by a noble family, as its feudal lord, until the family sold those rights to the British government. Under feudalism, land and the power to govern it could be held as a kind of inherited property, granted by a monarch.

A 1609 Act of Parliament gave the rights of Lord of Man to William Stanley, 6th Earl of Derby, and his heirs, and they came down to the Dukes of Atholl. An act passed in 1726 had already authorised the Treasury to make a purchase. Because Parliament had fixed the rights by law, it took another Act to end them. Under a contract with the Treasury, the Duke and Duchess of Atholl sold the rights to the Crown for £70,000 and an annuity, a fixed yearly payment, of £2,000 for their joint lives. The Isle of Man Purchase Act of 1765, also called the Act of Revestment, put this into effect on 10 May that year. Payment was due by 1 June. The government's reason was customs, since owning the island let it bring the island under the UK customs service and stop its use as a base for smuggling. A later account from the family says the Treasury first offered £40,000, which was refused, and that the final terms were accepted under the pressure of a bill already before Parliament.

The word revestment means putting something back into its earlier holder, here the Crown. Plans to merge the island into the English county of Cumberland met fierce local resistance, led by Sir George Moore, Speaker of the House of Keys, a chamber of the island's parliament, and did not go ahead.

The family kept its rights as local landlord, its power to choose the bishop and other privileges. Those went later under an Act of 1825, and they sold for £417,144 in 1828, though the Manx Notebook gives £416,000 in 1826. It shows that ruling rights could once be bought like property, but only because a higher authority, Parliament, had defined them and agreed to the transfer.
isle-of-man-revestment.why: Price was incomplete: the sale was £70,000 plus a £2,000 annuity, and the sellers were the Duke and Duchess jointly. Added the customs reason and the earlier offer.

liberia-cape-mesurado.story:
Liberia, in West Africa, grew from land acquired by a private American organisation, the American Colonization Society, which raised money to send free Black Americans to Africa. In the early 1800s free Black people in the United States faced severe legal discrimination and were not treated as citizens. Some opponents of slavery hoped emigration would help them. Slaveholders wanted free Black people out of their states, believing they threatened the stability of slave societies.

Its first ship left New York in 1820, with agents sent to find a site. In December 1821 they acquired Cape Mesurado, a 36-mile strip near present-day Monrovia, from a local ruler, King Peter, perhaps under some threat of force. The United States declined requests to make Liberia a colony or a formal protectorate, though it would intervene at times when Liberia's territory was threatened.

The colonists were attacked by the peoples whose territory it was, and suffered from disease and hunger. Only 1,819 of the 4,571 emigrants who arrived between 1820 and 1843 survived, the highest settler death rate reported in modern records. The colony spread along the coast and inland, sometimes by force, and other American colonisation societies set up their own settlements. Four settlements joined as the Commonwealth of Liberia in 1838. The Republic of Maryland, another settler state, stayed apart and was later forced to join Liberia by an insurgency of the Grebo and Kru peoples.

Under its first Black governor, Joseph Jenkins Roberts, Liberians voted in a referendum for independence, and eleven signers declared it on 26 July 1847. The society and some state governments continued to send money and emigrants into the 1870s. Roberts became the first president. Other governments took years to recognise the new state. Britain did so in 1848 and France in 1852. The United States did so only in 1862, after most Southern members of Congress, who had blocked it, left during the Civil War.

Liberia kept its independence through the European scramble for Africa. The descendants of the settlers, called Americo-Liberians, a small minority, controlled the country's politics until a violent overthrow in 1980, followed by two civil wars. It is one of the few cases of a private land purchase ending in a recognised state. Its settlers came to rule the peoples already living there.
liberia-cape-mesurado.why: Implied that all settlements merged in 1838, and omitted recognition, which is the point of the case for this subject.

lundy-harman.story:
Lundy is a small English island in the Bristol Channel, about 5 kilometres long and 19 kilometres off the coast of Devon, which has often been privately owned. The name comes from Old Norse and means puffin island. It had 28 residents in 2007. The businessman Martin Coles Harman bought it from the Christie family in 1924, along with its mail contract and a boat.

In 1929 he issued his own coins, the Half Puffin and the One Puffin, set equal in value to the British halfpenny and penny and named after the bird. Puffin stamps, sold as local carriage labels, remain a collector's item on the island.

Because Lundy was part of England, he was prosecuted under the Coinage Act of 1870. Devon magistrates fined him £5 with £15 15 shillings in costs in April 1930. He appealed to the High Court in 1931 and lost. The coins were withdrawn and became collector's items.

Harman owned the island and still could not issue money there. He never claimed that it was independent of the United Kingdom, although residents did not pay UK taxes and passed through customs on the way to and from it. He died in 1954, and after his son Albion died in 1968 the island was put up for sale. The millionaire Jack Hayward bought it in 1969 for £150,000 and gave it to the National Trust, a British conservation charity. The Landmark Trust now manages it and pays for it through day trips and holiday lets.
lundy-harman.why: Implied a direct passage from Harman to Hayward. Added Harman's death, the sale and price, and the fact that he never claimed independence.

puertopia-sol.story:
Puertopia, later renamed Sol, was a plan by wealthy cryptocurrency investors to build a new city in Puerto Rico, a US territory, in which the money would be virtual and contracts public. They arrived after Hurricane Maria hit in September 2017, as cryptocurrency prices were soaring. Their leader was Brock Pierce, director of the Bitcoin Foundation and co-founder of the blockchain firm Block.One.

The attraction was tax. The Irish Times described the island's offer to Americans who move there as no federal personal income tax, no capital gains tax and favourable business taxes, without giving up their citizenship. One member said they chose the island because the storm had swept everything away, leaving a case for rebuilding, and another investor called it a godsend in the long term.

In early 2018 they rented a 20,000-square-foot hotel in the capital, called the Monastery, as their base, and toured properties where they could have their own airports and docks. They debated buying the Roosevelt Roads Naval Station, 9,000 acres with two deep-water ports. Another resident said they had told him they would buy 250,000 acres and incorporate their own city. Some members thought moving into Old San Juan was enough. For the time being the governor was willing to speak at their conference, and they said they were close to permission for a cryptocurrency bank.

Their idea of a city was limited by law from the start, because the island remains under United States law. A local critic spoke of crypto colonialism, and another Puerto Rican called the island a tax playground for the rich. They are not known to have bought the base or founded a city.
puertopia-sol.why: The tax claim was stated as flat law but rests on one newspaper's summary. Now attributed. It should be checked against an IRS page, which could not be retrieved.

romanov-empire-bakov.story:
The Romanov Empire is a self-declared country, or micronation, with no land of its own, started in 2011 by Anton Bakov, a Russian businessman and former member of the Russian parliament from Yekaterinburg. He is chairman of a small monarchist party, and he says the project restores the Russian Empire. A writer once called him a political Leonardo for a run of unusual projects, including a local currency called the Ural franc.

The project began as the Imperial Throne. In 2014 it issued a manifesto naming the German prince Karl Emich of Leiningen as Emperor Nicholas III, and in 2017 it took the name Romanov Empire, with Bakov as Archchancellor. It sold passports online for 1,000 rubles, about $31, and claimed to have issued about 4,000 by 2014. In July 2013 Bakov said his state had granted citizenship to Edward Snowden, the former US intelligence contractor, who was then staying in Sheremetyevo Airport in Moscow.

To become a real state the project needed territory, so Bakov talked with several countries about buying land. As of 2017, talks with Kiribati and the Gambia had failed. Nicholas III also wrote to Vladimir Putin asking for land in Yekaterinburg for a capital, and that request was denied. A land purchase alone would bring private ownership only, unless the seller also gave up the right to rule.

In 2020 Bakov said a successor project called Arca Noë would be based on a floating settlement in neutral Mediterranean waters near Venice. It is not known to have been built. In January 2025 he told the media that he had set up an organisation called the Union of Gaza Developers and was negotiating to become a contractor for rebuilding the Gaza Strip.
romanov-empire-bakov.why: Added Bakov's most recent recorded project.

aland-settlement.story:
Åland is an archipelago between Finland and Sweden whose people speak Swedish. A convention of 30 March 1856 had already barred Russia from fortifying the islands, and during the First World War Russia did so anyway, to guard against a German invasion. After Finland became independent, Ålanders' wish to join Sweden became a dispute, and in 1921 the League of Nations ruled that Finland kept sovereignty and must grant the islands political autonomy.

Finland had passed an autonomy act dated 7 May 1920, replaced by new acts in 1951 and 1991. On 20 October 1921 Sweden, Finland and several other European countries signed a convention that guaranteed the islanders' rights to their language, culture and traditions and made Åland a neutral and demilitarised zone. The first regional assembly met on 9 June 1922.

Swedish is the only official language. A right of domicile passes from parent to child, and an immigrant may apply after five years with Finnish citizenship and enough Swedish. That right is needed to vote in Åland's parliamentary elections, to stand for them or to own rural land. A protocol to Finland's EU accession treaty lets Åland keep those limits, and Åland held its own referendum on joining in 1994.

The settlement is one of the longest-lasting examples of a treaty-backed autonomy. It gave a real community strong self-rule and control of who may hold land. It did this inside an existing state, by a decision of an international body, and the islands remained Finnish.
aland-settlement.why: The year 1916 and 'alarming Sweden' are not in the listed source, which says Russia remilitarised during the war against a feared German invasion.

boeing-sea-launch-export-penalty.story:
Export controls are national rules on who may receive weapons-related goods and know-how. The United States runs its version through the Arms Export Control Act and the International Traffic in Arms Regulations, usually called ITAR. The rules treat rocket technology as defence technology, so a US company sharing it with foreign partners needs a licence, and the technology has to be handled as the licence says.

Moving a rocket project onto the ocean does not change that, because the rules follow the company and the goods. Sea Launch tested this. Boeing managed the venture with partners in Russia, Ukraine and Norway. On 27 July 1998 the State Department suspended the project's export licences. Its Office of Defense Trade Controls found 207 violations between January 1994 and January 1998, in most cases because Boeing had not obtained prior approval of technology-transfer plans from the Defense Technology Security Administration.

Each violation could have brought a $500,000 penalty, $103.5 million in all, and a three-year bar. A Georgetown University case study frames the choice officials faced as cooperation with former rivals against the risk of leaking missile technology. Boeing agreed to a $10 million fine and a new document-control system, admitted no wrongdoing, and its licences were restored at the end of September. A criminal investigation was under way, and a Justice Department official said charges were unlikely because national security probably had not been breached.

No part of the company's position on the ocean affected any of this. For a project that hopes to build in open water, the case shows that a government can halt a launch programme by suspending its licences. Sea Launch went on to launch dozens of missions into orbit from a converted drilling rig, with its rig and vessels registered in Liberia. It shut down in 2014 after Russia's annexation of Crimea.
boeing-sea-launch-export-penalty.why: Added how the venture ended, from a source already listed.

decentraland-land.story:
Decentraland is an online 3D world, reached through a web browser, in which people buy plots of virtual land, build on them and walk around as cartoon figures called avatars. The Argentine developers Ari Meilich and Esteban Ordano began it in 2015. It is included because its plots are sold and spoken of as land, and it has its own currency and a form of self-rule.

A plot is a token, a unique digital ownership record on the Ethereum blockchain, a shared public ledger, and it is paid for in the world's currency, MANA. The company raised $26 million by selling MANA coins in 2017, when each coin cost two cents. The world opened to the public in February 2020 and is overseen by the nonprofit Decentraland Foundation, with users voting on policy.

The first map, Genesis City, has 90,601 plots, which sold for about $20 each at launch. There can be only that many, so scarcity is written into the code. During the 2021 cryptocurrency boom, plots sold for $6,000 to $100,000, and in November a virtual real-estate company paid $2.43 million for one. Use stayed small. The analytics firm DappRadar counted fewer than 1,000 users a day making transactions in October 2022, and as few as 38 on one day, while Decentraland claimed 8,000 daily users. Reviewers criticised its bugs and its mostly empty world.

Self-rule has limits of its own. In November 2021 a community vote on banning the name Hitler for avatars failed to get enough votes to take effect.

What a buyer gets is a record that says this token controls this square in this program. It carries no rights under any country's land law. There are no deeds in a county office and no police, and the plot exists only as long as the software keeps running. The buyer stays a resident and taxpayer of a real country. Decentraland remains open, and it released a test version of a new desktop program in October 2024. In November 2021 Barbados signed an agreement with Decentraland for what its foreign ministry called a metaverse embassy, using the language of territory for a place that has none of its legal effects.
decentraland-land.why: The Barbados claim was absent from the listed source. Added a source and the exact form of the announcement, and the 2024 release.

add_sources.t: Barbados Opens World's First Digital Embassy, CMC via Caribbean Today, 17 Nov 2021

elgaland-vargaland.story:
The Kingdoms of Elgaland-Vargaland is an art project in the form of a country. The Swedish artists Carl Michael von Hausswolff and Leif Elggren made its name from their own and announced it in an advertisement in the newspaper Dagens Nyheter on 27 May 1992. They named themselves kings, in reaction to the fact that Sweden still has a monarchy.

Its constitution claims what other countries leave out, which is the border zones between all countries on Earth, plus sea strips up to 10 nautical miles wide outside every country's territorial waters. It also claims states of mind and unreal places, including the Hypnagogic State, the moment between waking and sleep, and a digital Virtual Room. All dead people count as citizens, and it reported 980 living citizens in 2014.

In practice it runs as an art project does. The founders issue a flag, anthem, stamps and passports on request. They hold exhibitions called embassies, including in Reykjavik in 1994, Berlin in 2006 and Morocco in 2014. They applied for United Nations membership in 1994, and no result is known.

In 2002, for the tenth anniversary, a group of 10 travelled from Sweden to Estonia on its passports alone, planning to be turned away from one country after another. They were detained, their passports were confiscated and they were returned to Sweden the next day, which is the one moment the project met a real border. Its last dated activity is the embassy opened in Morocco in 2014.

Since a border in law is a line with no width, there is no strip of land to claim, and no state has to respond. The project shows how far a declaration can go when nobody has to answer it, and the Estonian episode shows where it stops.
elgaland-vargaland.why: Removed research narration and gave the Estonian episode as the source tells it.

liberland-metaverse.story:
Liberland is a self-declared country on Gornja Siga, an uninhabited stretch of floodplain on the Danube between Serbia and Croatia. The Czech activist Vít Jedlička declared it in 2015, arguing that the Croatia-Serbia border dispute left this patch unclaimed by either side. He describes a system of minimal government and an economy based on cryptocurrency. No state recognises it. Croatia and Serbia have both dismissed the claim as frivolous, and Serbia's foreign ministry treated it as a trivial matter that did not touch Serbian sovereignty. Croatia controls access, so supporters have had trouble even setting foot there. On 21 September 2023 Croatian police secured the site while wooden buildings put up by supporters were taken down, and made three arrests. Jedlička was banned from entering Croatia for five years.

A group that cannot reach its land can build somewhere else, and that was the point of the Liberland Metaverse. In early 2022 the architecture firm Zaha Hadid Architects, under its principal Patrik Schumacher, released designs for an online 3D city with curving buildings, a City Hall, a plaza and an exhibition centre, hosted on a platform called Mytaverse.

Buyers could purchase virtual land and set up businesses there, and they would also get a stake in the physical Liberland. Schumacher said the aim was to support Liberland's development as a libertarian micronation and to make a meeting place for cryptocurrency and online developers. He also argued that open virtual worlds run by their communities will beat those run by corporations. In November 2022 press reports still described Liberland as about to become a country in the metaverse. How many plots were sold, and whether the city is in use, is not known.

A virtual city gives people somewhere to gather and a project to invest in. It does nothing for the legal claim, which depends on whether real states accept Liberland and whether anyone can live on the floodplain.
liberland-metaverse.why: Serbia's position did not match the listed source. Added the 2023 police action, which bears on why a virtual site matters.

uae-iceberg-project.story:
The United Arab Emirates is a desert country on the Persian Gulf that depends heavily on machinery to turn seawater into drinking water. Icebergs are nearly pure frozen fresh water, and the idea of towing one has been around for decades. In 1977 Saudi Arabia's Prince Mohammad al Faisal set up a company, Iceberg Transport International, for the same purpose, and that plan was never carried out.

Abdulla Alsheni, an Emirati businessman who owned National Adviser Bureau Limited, announced a new version in 2017. An iceberg would come from the area of Heard Island in the Southern Ocean to the coast of Fujairah and might yield 20 billion gallons of water. He presented it to two UAE ministries, with a trial planned for early 2022 and a final tow in late 2023, at a cost of $100 to 150 million. An older timetable had set those steps for 2019 and 2020. The 2022 journal article on the project spells his name both Alsheni and Alshemi.

The legal question is who owns an iceberg. The project's website claimed that under the freedom of the high seas, the rule that open ocean belongs to no country, anyone may take icebergs for private use. In a 2022 article in the journal Ius Novum, the legal writer Mateusz Osiecki tested that claim. He concluded that a free-floating iceberg is probably no state's property, and he cited an earlier study by C. Lewis setting out three views, that an iceberg belongs to no one, that it can be property under a national claim, or that it is common property. He also set out the duties under the 1991 Environmental Protocol to the Antarctic Treaty, the rules protecting the Antarctic environment. He noted that the UAE is party to no instrument of the Antarctic Treaty system and has signed but not ratified the Law of the Sea treaty, the main agreement on the oceans. Treaties do not bind states outside them, though many of the sea treaty's rules are treated as customary law, which binds states whether they joined or not.

No treaty names the owner of a floating iceberg, and no court has ruled on the point. No tow is known to have taken place, so the argument remains untested. It belongs here as a case where ice is treated as a resource to be taken, the reverse of treating it as a place to live.
uae-iceberg-project.why: UAE signed UNCLOS but did not ratify it, and the article qualifies the point through customary law. The three views are from a study he cites. Name spelling varies inside the source.

akon-city.story:
Akon City was a planned futuristic city on the coast of Senegal in West Africa, in the M'bour Department. Its promoter was the singer Akon, born Aliaune Thiam in the United States and partly raised in Senegal. He announced it in June 2018 at the Cannes Lions advertising festival, saying that it would run on his own cryptocurrency, Akoin, and that President Macky Sall had given him 2,000 acres, about 800 hectares.

It was not a claim to independence. It was a special development within Senegal, and its land rested on a deal with the state. On 13 January 2020 Akon signed a memorandum of understanding, a preliminary agreement, with Sapco, Senegal's state tourism development body, in the presence of the tourism minister. A groundbreaking ceremony followed in August 2020. The reported cost was $6 billion, to come mainly from American private partners, with a first phase by 2023 and completion by 2029. Commentators compared the curving tower designs with Wakanda from the Black Panther films.

The city did not appear on schedule. A welcome centre was under construction at the site in December 2023, and by June 2024 only the frame of that one curved building stood. On 28 June 2024 Sapco sent Akon a formal notice that the land would be reclaimed if construction did not begin by the end of July, and Bloomberg reported that he had missed several payments to the agency. In 2025 the head of Sapco, Serigne Mamadou Mboup, told the BBC that the Akon City project no longer exists. He said Akon and Sapco had agreed on a more realistic project that Sapco would support. According to Domus, the government revoked nearly all the land, Akon keeps about 8 hectares, and Sapco plans a $1.2 billion resort at Mbodiène with hotels, a marina and housing.

A government's backing and a famous name gave this project attention, but they did not produce the money. Since the land came through a state agency, the agency could change the deal when nothing was built. The city's private money and its private currency could not change that, because its legal base was a preliminary paper with the Senegalese state.
akon-city.why: Missing the formal notice, the land being revoked and the replacement resort, which are what show the agency's power. Status was empty.

add_sources.t: From Wakanda to resort: Akon's futuristic city in Senegal canceled, Domus, Jul 2025

deepsea-ventures-claim.story:
Far out on the deep Pacific floor lie manganese nodules, potato-sized lumps containing copper, nickel, cobalt and manganese. They sit thousands of metres down, well beyond any country's waters. By the 1970s companies believed they might one day be worth mining. The law had almost nothing to say about them. The ocean floor had seen little commercial use apart from undersea cables, and the Law of the Sea treaty, the main international agreement on use of the oceans, was still being negotiated. In June 1974 the ship Hughes Glomar Explorer, said to belong to the billionaire Howard Hughes, sailed from Long Beach, reportedly to mine nodules. That story was false. The ship was secretly backed by the US Central Intelligence Agency, which used it to recover part of a sunken Soviet submarine, K-129, and mining was the cover. Hughes and his companies had no real part in the project.

Deepsea Ventures Inc. of Gloucester Point, Virginia, decided to try to establish a right before anyone wrote the rules. On 15 November 1974 its president, John Flipse, sent Secretary of State Henry Kissinger a "Notice of Discovery and Claim of Exclusive Mining Rights, and Request for Diplomatic Protection and Protection of Investment". He also recorded a copy at the Gloucester County Circuit Court, an ordinary local court where property papers are filed. Copies went by registered mail to cabinet members, congressional committees, ambassadors of maritime countries, oceanographers and other companies. The idea was publicity. The older rule for unowned things is that whoever finds and takes them first has a claim, and the company wanted everyone to be on notice that it had found this deposit first.

The tract covered 60,000 square kilometres of the northeastern Pacific. The company promised commercial production within 15 years, running for 40 years. It claimed exclusive rights to mine and sell the nodules, and it took care to say that it was claiming no territory and was not asking the United States to do so. That distinction reflects the rule that nobody could own the high seas. It wanted a right to the minerals, in the way someone may have a right to fish from a sea no one owns. The magazine Reason called it the world's first ocean mining claim and argued that the minerals were unclaimed property for whoever made the effort.

The legal ground then shifted. By 1979 Congress was considering a bill to let the US government license seabed mining by itself. The 1982 treaty put the seabed outside national zones under an international authority and declared that no one may own it by claiming it. Mining is not known to have taken place under the claim, and no court is known to have ruled on it. The case is the clearest early try at a private claim outside any country, and it shows why such a claim needed a government's protection, which is what Flipse asked Kissinger for.
deepsea-ventures-claim.why: The Glomar Explorer's mining voyage was stated without saying it was a CIA cover story. Added the US licensing bill. Status was empty.

metals-company.story:
The Metals Company is a Canadian-founded business that wants to mine metal-rich nodules from the Pacific floor. It began as DeepGreen Metals in 2011. The nodules, which contain nickel, copper, cobalt and manganese, lie in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, between Mexico and Hawaii, on seabed that no country owns. Under the Law of the Sea treaty, that seabed is controlled by the International Seabed Authority, and a company needs a contract with the authority and a sponsoring member country.

The company worked within that system by using small Pacific states. Its subsidiary NORI held an exploration contract sponsored by Nauru, and it later bought TOML, sponsored by Tonga. In 2012 DeepGreen agreed to sell 50 percent of its future nickel and copper from the NORI area to the commodity trader Glencore. In 2021 it merged with a listed shell company, a firm with a stock listing and no business, in a $2.9 billion deal, and took its current name.

In June 2021 Nauru told the authority that it intended to begin mining. A rule in the treaty system meant that this started a two-year deadline to finish the mining rules. The deadline passed and the rules were not finished, which left the company with exploration rights and no way to mine.

It then turned to another route. The United States never joined the treaty, and it has its own older law on seabed mining. On 24 April 2025 President Trump signed an order telling the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the American ocean agency, to speed up permits under that law. Within days the company's American arm applied. NOAA found on 28 April 2026 that the application met the law's information requirements. On 19 August 2026 it opened a 60-day public comment period, which ran to 19 October, with an online public hearing on 13 October. Comments feed into its decision on whether to certify the application, and after that come an environmental impact statement and a final decision on whether to issue the permit. No permit had been issued by August. In its second-quarter 2026 report the company said NOAA's review had slipped by a few months and that it still expected the permit before commissioning its offshore collection system, targeted for the end of 2027.

The authority responded by opening an inquiry into whether NORI and TOML had broken their contracts. The two companies took it to a specialist chamber of the international law of the sea tribunal in June 2026, and on 18 July the chamber ordered the authority to respect fair procedure, without suspending the inquiry. The main case is undecided. NORI's contract was extended to 2031, and TOML's runs to January 2027 with an extension pending.

The company stands on both sides of the question. Its subsidiaries hold contracts under the treaty, and its American arm seeks a permit that would bypass that treaty. The United States told the authority in July 2026, by the company's account, that it is not bound by the treaty's seabed mining rules. What remains open is whether one country's permit can give a company a right to mine an area that most of the world has agreed to manage together. The answer will affect anyone hoping to operate outside the shared system with one government's approval.
